Putting aside the wildness of that (but what does it mean?) I learned a few lessons as I cruised through the five boroughs for the seventh time.
Specifically, although I ran the exact same time, my splits looked quite different. I ran the latter miles faster and they felt easier this year. And that comes down to one key training adjustment I made: adding more overall mileage to my week.
Here’s how and why I maximized my volume during this training cycle, and how it paid off in my strongest finish yet (even if not a PR).
How I Increased My Weekly Mileage
I ran the London Marathon in April, and both New York and Sydney last year, using an artificial intelligence training app. I programmed in that I wanted to run three days a week so I could continue to strength train two to three days a week as well. Plus, I walk quite a bit as someone who lives in New York City (around four to five miles a day on top of any running).
But then I reported on a series of articles about durability for Runner’s World and I started thinking more about total weekly mileage and how much I had (or had not) been doing. Turns out, I peaked around 30 to 35 miles for all three of those marathons. It made me realize there was room for growth.
When I got the opportunity to run New York again this year, I figured out how high I could go mileage-wise without upping my risk for injury.
I started by talking to Andrew Kastor, head coach of the Asics Mammoth Track Club. Before our call, I sent him the training plan I planned to follow for this upcoming training cycle: the Runner’s World Break Four Hours plan. (I also intended to continue strength training twice a week.)
The peak week mileage for that plan: 48 miles, with at least four days a week of running. This may not seem like a ton to people who swear by super high mileage, but it is a steep increase relative to my previous builds. “Between 32 and 50 is night and day,” Kastor says. “You’re going to notice a big difference in your staying power after mile 20.”
Importantly, I built a pretty solid base before starting the training plan 16 weeks out from race day and felt ready to jump into week one when the time came. This plan also leverages mileage ranges, rather than firm numbers, allowing me to further customize it.
Kastor likes the approach of mileage ranges and uses it with many of his athletes. “It kind of takes a little bit of the edge off or the pressure off,” he says, because you can choose the lower end of the range if you’re feeling fatigued.
He also advised me to add in the optional up-to-three-mile run in my plan every other week (where you see 0 to 3 miles). “It’ll be worth it the last mile of the race or the last two miles of the race [when] you’re able to hold that 9:07 pace or that nine flat pace,” he says.

AST SpaceMobile Is Building Its Own Reusable Rocket to Rely Less on SpaceX
AST SpaceMobile wants its own rocket, and Firefly is cashing in before a single engine fires. The deal could cost shareholders more than dilution, and the satellites that actually earn revenue still sit on the ground.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Before the open on November 6, 2026, AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) said it will build its own rocket, Blacklift, to launch its BlueBird satellites starting in late 2028. Firefly Aerospace (NASDAQ:FLY | FLY Price Prediction) will supply the engines.
Firefly last traded at $20.76, up 36.8%. AST fell to a new 52-week low of $27.58 and then turned higher to $32.33, up 7.05%.
Launching its own rocket would let AST rely less on SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX). The cost is a capital-heavy rocket program at a company still working to get its satellites into orbit and earn revenue.
What AST Actually Committed To
AST says Blacklift is designed to be reused and to carry up to five BlueBirds per launch. The company’s headline calls it a 20-ton rocket but does not say whether that number refers to payload.
The rocket does not exist yet, and the late-2028 target is ambitious. AST plans to unveil it in New York on November 12.
AST gets a permanent license to build Firefly’s Miranda engine and Vira, its vacuum version, at a new U.S. engine plant. President Scott Wisniewski said Miranda lets AST “leapfrog the traditional five-to-ten-year development cycle.”
How AST Pays for Its Engines
Firefly Aerospace values the deal at more than $1.3 billion over three years. That covers 27 Miranda and nine Vira engines for AST’s first three rockets, plus the license and engineering support. Firefly keeps engine intellectual property.
The license costs about $800 million upfront: $400 million in cash plus 10 million to 14 million AST Class A shares. The share count depends on a forward volume-weighted average price, the stock’s average trading price over a future period weighted by volume. If AST’s stock is weaker during that period, Firefly gets more shares.
AST then pays $250 million for engines and $250 million for three years of engineering support. The shares come with lock-ups, but they still dilute current holders.
Why Firefly Posted Its Biggest Gain Since Its Debut
By daily closes, this was Firefly’s biggest gain since it began trading on August 7, 2025. It beat the 22.8% gain on December 19, 2025, and the 34.1% first-day rise above its IPO price.
The jump shows the deal’s size, which is worth about 37% of Firefly’s $3.48 billion market value and about 4.5 times its trailing revenue of $287.01 million.
Even after the jump, the stock sits about 54% below its $45 IPO price. Firefly reports on November 10 and will discuss the deal on a 5 p.m. ET call.
Where AST’s Rocket Plan Could Stall
AST has bought launches from SpaceX, India’s space agency, and Blue Origin. It still holds launch agreements covering more than 100 BlueBirds through 2027 and 2028. Blacklift would help AST rely less on those providers, and the release names no provider it plans to drop.
Rocket programs often slip. This one adds cash burn and dilution at a company that lost $230.91 million in the second quarter, and it could take attention away from putting satellites in orbit, which is the business that has to produce revenue.

He Inherited 8,000 IBM Shares Worth Nearly $2 Million at 52. The Often Overlooked IRS Rule That Decides Whether Most of It Is Taxed as Income or a Capital Gain
Inheriting a 401(k) stuffed with company stock sounds like a windfall until the standard rollover form arrives. One signature can decide whether nearly $2 million gets taxed at the highest rates, and most heirs only learn the alternative after it's…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
If your parent left you a 401(k) full of company stock, the default paperwork could cost you a fortune. A little-known IRS rule called net unrealized appreciation (NUA) lets an heir take employer stock out of an inherited 401(k) and pay capital gains tax on most of it instead of ordinary income tax. Most heirs never hear about it until the money has already moved.
A Hypothetical $2 Million Inheritance Inside a 401(k)
This example is hypothetical. It exists to show how the rule works. A son, 52, is the named beneficiary of his late father’s 401(k). The father spent 33 years as a systems engineer at IBM (NYSE:IBM | IBM Price Prediction) and bought IBM stock inside the plan throughout his career. Those purchases, plus IBM’s two-for-one stock splits declared in January 1997 and January 1999 (per IBM’s filings), left the plan holding 8,000 shares with a cost basis of $231,000.
At IBM’s price of $244.89 as of 2:37 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, the shares are worth $1,959,120. That leaves $1,728,120 of net unrealized appreciation, or 88.2% of the position. The value moves with IBM’s stock price.
Two Paths, Two Very Different Tax Bills
The default: an inherited IRA. Most heirs roll the balance into an inherited IRA. The son is more than 10 years younger than his father, so he falls outside the eligible designated beneficiary category for someone “not more than 10 years younger” than the owner. That means he must empty the account by the end of the tenth year after the year his father died, per the IRS. Every dollar he withdraws, growth included, counts as ordinary income.
The overlooked option: a lump-sum distribution. The IRS treats a payout made “Because of the plan participant’s death” as a lump-sum distribution if the entire balance comes out within a single tax year. The son takes the IBM shares in kind, moving them as stock into a taxable brokerage account. IRS Publication 575 explains the result: “employer stock basis is taxed as ordinary income and appreciation is taxed later at capital gains rates.” The NUA “is generally tax free until you sell or exchange the securities.”
In this example, he reports $231,000 as ordinary income in the year of the distribution. The $1,728,120 of appreciation goes untaxed until he sells. At that point, The CPA Journal notes, it counts as a long-term capital gain.
Where the Rule Lives in the Tax Code
NUA treatment comes from 26 U.S.C. § 402(e)(4), which covers employer securities paid out of qualified plans. IRS Publication 575 lays out how it works. The CPA Journal points out how easy it is to miss: “NUA can frequently be overlooked when taxpayers look to consolidate older plans into one IRA or even at death when an heir is named the designated beneficiary of the plan.”

The total comprised $822 million in current expected credit loss, or CECL, reserves and $217 million in reserves on real estate owned. DiModica said most of the increase was driven by higher interest rates incorporated into a third-party model. Higher projected rates can increase borrowers’ debt-service costs and reduce refinancing proceeds, even when property operations improve, he said. Substantially all of the increase was in the general reserve.
The balance of loans rated four increased by $290 million, while five-rated loans rose by $440 million. All downgrades during the quarter involved loans originated before 2023, and more than half involved multifamily properties, DiModica said.

Starwood resolved $254 million of non-accrual loans and real estate owned during the quarter, Paniry said. The sales were completed in cash without seller financing.

For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth.
That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it.
Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they're still in school.
At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes.
There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them.
Decisions are coming earlier
Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made.
The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust?
These aren't professional athlete questions. They're life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before.
One thing I've learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan's Athlete Center of Excellence is that they're eager for this guidance.
I've spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I've seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant.
Athletes need to think like CEOs
Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts.
Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions.
I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don't have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future.
That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today's athletes aren't just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age.
The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it.

Choosing between established giants and high-growth disruptors remains a classic dilemma for investors. For those interested in exposure to the tech industry, deciding whether the steady cash generation of Adobe (ADBE -2.90%) or the accelerating momentum of Palantir Technologies (PLTR +3.48%) can be a challenge, as both have different pros and cons.
Adobe provides the software tools for digital creativity, while Palantir focuses on data integration and decision-making software. Both companies are now racing to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into their core offerings to capture a larger share of enterprise spending.
The case for Adobe
Adobe sells a comprehensive suite of digital tools through various platforms targeting different customer segments. It serves a diverse audience, including professional designers, students, and large global enterprises that rely on its proprietary formats. The company has integrated its Firefly generative artificial intelligence models directly into its software, helping users create content more efficiently.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), ended last Nov. 28, revenue reached $23.8 billion, representing a revenue growth of 10.5% compared to the previous year. The company reported a net income of $7.1 billion, which reflects a healthy net margin of 30%. This growth is supported by a sticky subscription model that provides predictable recurring revenue from its massive base of over one billion monthly active users.
As of its November 2025 balance sheet, Adobe maintains a stable financial position with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.6x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to measure financial leverage. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, stands at 1.0x. During the same period, the company generated $9.9 billion in free cash flow, providing significant capital for reinvestment or acquisitions.
The case for Palantir Technologies
Palantir Technologies builds sophisticated software solutions, such as its artificial intelligence platform (AIP), that help organizations analyze complex data. Its strategy involves securing long-term contracts with government agencies and expanding rapidly into the commercial sector with partnerships like Amerilife and Changshin. The company positions AIP as a central operating system that allows businesses to deploy large language models (LLMs) safely and effectively.
In FY 2025, ended Dec. 31, revenue reached $4.5 billion, marking a significant revenue growth of 56.2% over the prior year. This acceleration helped the company achieve a net income of $1.6 billion, resulting in a net margin of 36.3%. The rapid expansion in the commercial segment has become a primary driver of overall growth, as more businesses seek to modernize their data operations.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Palantir Technologies carries a debt-to-equity ratio of zero, indicating it has very little debt relative to its equity. Its current ratio is 7.1x, which suggests a very high level of liquidity for its daily operations. The company generated $2.1 billion in free cash flow in FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 32% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Key Takeaways
- Qualcomm rose 5.5% Friday after Alphabet disclosed a $548 million stake, days after weak handset sales hit the stock following earnings.
- Handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion, while automotive revenue jumped 89% to a record $1.99 billion.
- CEO Cristiano Amon expects handset units to stay flat to down in calendar 2027, putting the burden on data centers and cars.
- The February 3 report, guided to $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion of revenue, is the next test.
Qualcomm (QCOM) got a vote of confidence from a new data center partner on Friday.
Alphabet (GOOGL) disclosed a $548 million stake in the chipmaker, and the shares rose 5.5% to $165. It came days after Qualcomm announced a multi-generational product collaboration with Amazon (AMZN) for AI data centers.
The bounce followed a rough week. Qualcomm slumped after its November 4 report as weak smartphone chip sales overshadowed data center momentum, and the broad chip selloff on November 5 piled on.
Even after Friday, the stock is down 13% over six months and 36% below its $260 52-week high.
Handsets fell, cars took off
The quarter split cleanly in two.
- Non-GAAP EPS of $2.17 edged past the $2.16 estimate but fell 28% from $3.00.
- Handset revenue dropped 26% to $5.14 billion.
- Automotive revenue rose 89% to a record $1.99 billion, its first quarter near $2 billion.
GAAP revenue fell 8% to $10.32 billion. Restructuring charges, mostly severance, pulled GAAP EPS down to $1.17.
Total revenue shows how much handsets still dominate…
Revenue has now fallen year over year for consecutive quarters, so cars and data centers have a big hole to fill.
Betting on non-handset growth
Amon says the turn starts now. “Fiscal 2027 marks the start of our non-handset revenue inflection, including the ramp of our Data Center business,” he said in the earnings release.
Management projects non-handset revenue to grow more than 60% in fiscal 2027 and reiterated a $5 billion data center revenue target for the year. Qualcomm also renewed long-term licensing deals with Apple, Huawei and Transsion, which steadies the royalty side.
Alphabet’s stake is a signal more than a financial event. At $548 million, it equals about 0.3% of Qualcomm’s $177 billion market value.
Handsets will keep hurting. Amon said on the call that the plan assumes global handset units will remain flat to down in calendar 2027.
Can consensus growth survive that?
Analysts expect about 10% annual revenue growth over the next two years. That forecast leans heavily on the data center ramp showing up on time.

Cheap, with a margin catch
Qualcomm trades at 16.7x forward earnings with a 2.3% dividend yield. Wall Street’s average target of $186 implies 12% upside.

We just published the list of the 10 Worst Dow Stocks To Buy, and IBM (NYSE:IBM) ranks 9th on this list.
Yahoo Finance reported on November 5 that the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 3.4%, or more than 1,800 points, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5% into correction territory. Chip stocks took the brunt of the damage, as the leading AI chipmaker fell 9% to pace Dow decliners and another chip designer plunged 17%, the outlet reported.
The slide erased the gains from a day earlier, when the Dow had jumped nearly 1,600 points after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, Yahoo Finance wrote on November 4. Even so, the blue-chip index finished Thursday just 1.9% below its record closing high of 54,349 from early August, according to Yahoo Finance.
The Dow's Safe-Haven Run Cracks
For most of the week the Dow had looked like the sheltered corner of the market. Yahoo Finance reported on November 2 that the Dow edged up 0.4% while the Nasdaq dropped roughly 1% as investors rotated out of technology names and into consumer cyclical and financial services shares. One household consumer brand has divided opinion lately, and we covered why a well-known TV host is staying away from the sneaker maker after losing money on it.
On Thursday that cushion gave way, as the focus turned to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI buildout, and for the data centers driving it in particular, according to Yahoo Finance. Data center power and infrastructure stocks fell by double digits, and the Nasdaq 100 was recently more than 10% below its October closing high.
The reversal was fast. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at an equity research firm, pointed out that the VIX volatility index posted its biggest one-day jump in more than two years, Yahoo Finance reported on November 5. It took the Nasdaq just six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally.
A Jobs Report Steadies the Tape
Friday brought a partial rebound. Yahoo Finance reported on November 6 that the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, and the Nasdaq gained 1.9% while the S&P 500 rose 1% and the Dow added 0.1%. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why a billionaire money manager and a TV host both still like the iPhone maker.
The stronger jobs data lifted Treasury yields and kept Federal Reserve policy at the center of market attention, Reuters reported on November 6, as the price-weighted index of 30 major U.S. companies held roughly flat.

It might be difficult for some of us, but think about the 1950s for a moment. Specifically, the year 1955. What's significant about that year?
It's the year in which Procter & Gamble (PG -1.02%) started raising its dividend, a streak that remains alive and well today at 71 years. Not only does that make the consumer staples Goliath a Dividend King, or one of the corporations with a payout-increase streak of at least 50 years, it also means the Tide maker is tied for the third-largest dividend-increase streak among U.S. companies.
Think about that. Procter & Gamble's run of consecutive dividend increases is nearly as old as color television, predates the Moon landing by 14 years, and began nearly 20 years before women could get credit cards without a male co-signer. In other words, Procter & Gamble's devotion to steady dividend hikes puts the "long" in "longevity."
Durable in trying economic environments
Call it certainty, consistency, or dependability, but those are very much the reasons why so many investors embrace Dividend Kings, including Procter & Gamble. Market participants certainly love all-weather durability, which the Febreze maker has.
Think about P&G's dividend reliability in the context of recessions. The experts at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) say there have been 10 official recessions since 1955. Some, such as the COVID-19 economic contraction of 2020, were brief. Others, including the 1981-82 recession and the global financial crisis earlier this century, lasted well over a year.
Through all of that, good times and bad, Procter & Gamble's dividend ticked higher every year. That's the type of dependability that dividend growth investors should prioritize. The consumer defensive label isn't a guarantee against future negative action. Some of the sector's previously storied names have cut payouts.

However, Procter & Gamble's dividend is considered safe, and its payout ratio of 67.8% of free cash flow isn't alarmingly high, particularly when accounting for one of the highest levels of free cash flow in the household products industry. Those are among the reasons why I'm bullish on P&G heading into 2027, even though the stock is up 16% year to date.
More reasons to like P&G in 2027
Indeed, P&G stock is hot this year, but it can keep the good times rolling in 2027, particularly if jitters about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade linger. The U.S. Election Day rebuke of data centers in some states may be a sign that some investors will lean into defensive stocks heading into the new year.
Speaking of Election Day, congressional power changed hands. That's not necessarily an alarm bell for investors, but uncertainty about how legislative agendas will shape up could compel market participants to gravitate toward lower-volatility names, such as P&G.
There's talk that the new congressional majority could push through new spending initiatives, potentially stoking inflation.
